edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5 Availability, Detect Faults tactic tree
edges.note: Bass refines Exception Detection into system exception, parameter fence, parameter typing, timeout.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, Exception Detection refinement
edges.note: Parameter typing is a named refinement of Exception Detection in Bass's tactic tree.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, Exception Detection refinement
edges.note: Timeout (timing-constraint exception) is a sub-tactic of Exception Detection.
Two sibling ways to detect corrupt/mismatched parameters: memory guard pattern vs TLV type agreement.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, Recover-Preparation tactics
edges.note: Exception handling acts only after an exception has been detected; it depends on detection.
Prevent exceptions from arising at all vs detect-then-handle them; different responses to the same class of faults.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, Monitor tactic
edges.note: A system monitor coordinates detection tactics; ping/echo is a mechanism it drives to check reachability.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, Monitor/Heartbeat tactics
edges.note: Heartbeats are emitted to a system monitor, which detects failure from their absence.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, Self-Test tactic
edges.note: Self-test can be invoked periodically by the system monitor to check component health.
The monitor employs condition checks (e.g. checksums) as one of the health-detection mechanisms it coordinates.
The monitor applies reasonableness checks on component outputs at interfaces as a detection mechanism.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, Ping/Echo and Heartbeat tactics
edges.note: Both detect liveness; ping/echo is initiated by the monitor, heartbeat by the monitored component.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, Ping/Echo tactic
edges.note: Ping/echo declares failure after a time threshold on the echo, i.e. it relies on a timeout.
Absence of the periodic heartbeat is detected by a watchdog timer / timeout expiring.
Sibling detect-faults tactics: check output reasonableness at interfaces vs check internal conditions/assumptions.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, Voting tactic (replication/functional/analytic redundancy)
edges.note: Analytic redundancy is one of the redundancy variants Bass lists under the Voting tactic.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, Voting tactic
edges.note: Functional redundancy diversifies design only; analytic redundancy also diversifies inputs/outputs — competing redundancy schemes.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, Voting tactic
edges.note: TMR is described as the most common realization of the Voting tactic; it depends on a voter.
MooN architecture generalizes the voting tactic to an m-of-n agreement threshold.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, Voting tactic
edges.note: Voting compares results from replicated components, so it depends on replication to produce the candidates.
Voting/comparison identifies a divergent source whose subsequent messages are then ignored as spurious.
A source is judged spurious (e.g. a failed sensor) via sanity/reasonableness checks before ignoring it.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, Spare / redundancy tactics
edges.note: Failover switches service to a standby, so it depends on a configured redundant spare.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, State Resynchronization tactic
edges.note: For clean takeover the standby's state must be resynchronized with the active unit.
Loss of heartbeat/ping from the active unit is the trigger that initiates switchover to the standby.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, State Resynchronization tactic
edges.note: Hot/warm spares stay ready via state resync (checksum comparison or periodic state transfer).

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, Software Upgrade tactic
edges.note: Hitless in-service software upgrade is built on redundant spares that take the load during the upgrade.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, Shadow / Software Upgrade tactics
edges.note: A freshly upgraded component is run in shadow mode to validate it before it takes an active role.
In-service function/class patching vs swapping whole environments: two ways to upgrade without downtime.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, Shadow tactic
edges.note: Shadow mode lets a returning component repopulate/resynchronize its state before it is restored to service.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, Non-Stop Forwarding tactic
edges.note: While the data plane keeps forwarding, the control-plane routing state is rebuilt and resynchronized.
Keep forwarding on the data plane through a control-plane fault vs switching the whole node to a standby.
Both recover by resetting a component to scrub latent faults; escalating restart chooses the granularity of the reset.

edges.cite: Armstrong, 'Programming Erlang' / OTP supervisor design principles
edges.note: OTP supervision trees restart failed children at escalating scope (one-for-one up to whole subtree).

edges.cite: Candea & Fox, 'Crash-Only Software' (HotOS 2003) / microreboot
edges.note: Crash-only design enables fine-grained microreboots, the least-disruptive levels of escalating restart.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, Prevent Faults tactics
edges.note: A predictive model can trigger rejuvenation/removal-from-service before latent faults become failures.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, Predictive Model tactic
edges.note: The predictive model is employed together with monitoring of operational metrics to forecast faults.
Predictions are drawn from monitored conditions (threshold crossings, queue lengths, process state).

edges.cite: Nygard, 'Release It!' (2nd ed.), Stability Patterns (Timeouts, retries)
edges.note: Bounded retries are gated by timeouts so a hung call fails fast before the next attempt.
After reverting to a known-good checkpoint the operation is retried, assuming the fault was transient.
Retry the same unit (transient fault) vs switch to a redundant standby (persistent fault): rival recovery choices.
Transaction semantics give the atomic, all-or-nothing revert to the last consistent state that rollback needs.
Both keep critical function alive under failure: reconfiguration remaps work, degradation drops non-critical function — used together.
Remap the logical architecture onto surviving resources vs switch the failed unit to a dedicated spare.
Throttling sheds/rejects excess requests as a controlled form of degradation that protects critical SLA.
Both are prevent-faults tactics reducing the number of conditions that ever become exceptions.
Absorb edge states as normal operation vs raise-and-handle them as exceptions: two responses to the same states.

edges.cite: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, Throttling & Queue-Based Load Leveling pattern pages
edges.note: Azure pairs them: routing requests through a leveling queue is a way to implement throttling and smooth load.

edges.cite: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, Queue-Based Load Leveling / Competing Consumers pattern pages
edges.note: Azure recommends combining them: multiple competing consumers drain the leveling queue to scale processing.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Ch.5, Transactions tactic
edges.note: Distributed ACID transactions are most commonly realized via a two-phase commit protocol.
A rejuvenated component runs self-tests to confirm correct operation before being returned to service.
Timestamps/sequence numbers detect stale or misordered state so resynchronization applies the newest version.
Timestamp/sequence ordering supports the consistency and serialization that transaction semantics enforce.
